# Commitment Spiral

A 36-week fictional capacity model. The opening view compares one intervention at two start weeks against a frozen reference course. Move the start sliders or drag across the chart to inspect a week; selecting a causal step changes the plotted quantity and its explanation. Usable output and declined demand stay visible together. Additional consequences and the original custom policy sequence open progressively.

`timing.js` copies the current course’s policy schedule and shared-history week. Both variations hold one selected lever at the chosen value from their start through week 36. All other levers retain their exact scheduled changes, including future events. The original custom course and pinned baseline remain intact. Editing that course does not silently change the timing reference; **Use current custom course as reference** copies it explicitly, retaining the selected lever and amount. A and B may start in either order or the same week. Reset/scenario changes create a new reference. Changing model assumptions recomputes all courses under the same assumptions.

The full controls still run, step, schedule policies and fork a baseline. The default custom course opens at week 6; reset returns to week 0. Every branch shares the same stateless seeded demand sequence. Chart paths beyond the reference week and week-36 outcomes are hypothetical continuations, not observations or empirical forecasts.

Three levers control accepted demand, resistance to shortcuts, and protected recovery. Weekly effort balances across delivery, returned repairs, reporting, recovery and idle time. Fatigue reduces the following week’s capacity. Overdue promises and lower trust add reporting work. Shortcut defects return two weeks after delivery; repair costs 1.7 effort points per defective point by default. Usable output subtracts known and hidden outstanding defects. The timing trace exposes actual computed quantities; it does not attribute the whole result to one isolated pathway. Shortcut savings are shown as avoided effort per delivery, not a made-up success score. The capacity trace uses ending fatigue to calculate next-week capacity, including the implied week 37 at the horizon.

**Challenge the model** changes repair cost (0.5–4), maximum capacity loss from fatigue (0–75%), and direct reporting effort per 10 overdue points (0–1.5). Defaults: 1.7, 45%, 0.65. Applying assumptions pauses and replays custom, baseline and timing courses from week 1, preserving their policies and shared demand. Ordinary and trust-related reporting remain when the direct lateness cost is zero. Settings persist through scenario/reset actions until restored.

Work is divisible and homogeneous, with a common two-week promise window. Coefficients, trust and fatigue scales are illustrative. Demand does not respond to trust. No pricing, strategic value of commitments, hiring, cancellation or renegotiation. Declined demand has no invented value. Lower promise rates can preserve later output under pressure and lose useful output under gentle demand. Colours identify courses rather than recommending a winner.

`engine.js` is pure. `step` and `simulate` retain their optional fourth assumptions argument. New trace fields expose pressure, starting backlog and prior fatigue without changing the equations. `thinking-lab:commitment:v1` keeps its original custom-session fields, adding optional validated `timing` settings and a frozen policy schedule. Old saves retain their custom week, events, baseline and assumptions. Markdown includes both custom and timing courses, reference policies, conditions, outcomes and the selected mechanism/week.

Run `node --test dist/commitment/*.test.js`. Tests cover conservation, feedback delays, matching histories/demand, preservation of other scheduled levers, equal-date/no-change counterexamples, next-week capacity, source independence and portable timing context. Browser journeys cover desktop/phone, touch start changes and chart scrubbing, keyboard focus, existing saved sessions, reference refresh, shared assumption changes, reload and Markdown download.

Feature-detected WebMCP tools retain their current-state, policy-scheduling and simulation controls through `document.modelContext.registerTool`, with a navigator fallback. The read state includes timing settings. Synchronous/asynchronous registration failures are contained; native browser support remains unconfirmed. No network or external dependencies.
